difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: MODERATE — one concept (Taylor polynomial) that needs logarithmic differentiation and a product rule for the second derivative, then a short substitution; about 2 minutes.
concept: Degree-2 Taylor polynomial of $x^{x}$ about $x=1$ via logarithmic differentiation
stem:
Let $f(x) = x^{x}$ for $x > 0$, and let $P_2(x)$ be the Taylor polynomial of degree $2$ of $f$ about $x = 1$.

The value of $P_2(1.2)$ is

steps.title: First derivative by logarithmic differentiation
steps.body:
Write $f(x) = x^{x} = e^{x\ln x}$. Since $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\ln x) = \ln x + 1$,

$$f'(x) = x^{x}\,(\ln x + 1).$$

steps.title: Second derivative by the product rule
steps.body:
Differentiate $f'(x) = f(x)\,(\ln x + 1)$ as a product:

$$f''(x) = f'(x)(\ln x + 1) + f(x)\cdot\frac{1}{x} = x^{x}\left[(\ln x + 1)^{2} + \frac{1}{x}\right].$$

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: $1.20$ is the linear approximation $1 + (x-1)$ evaluated at $1.2$; it leaves out the quadratic term $(x-1)^2$ altogether.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: $1.22$ comes from taking $f''(1) = 1$, i.e. forgetting the $\tfrac{1}{x}$ term produced by the product rule. The coefficient of $(x-1)^2$ would then be $\tfrac12$, giving $1 + 0.2 + 0.02$.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: Correct. With $f''(1) = 2$ the quadratic coefficient is $\tfrac{2}{2!} = 1$, so $P_2(1.2) = 1 + 0.2 + 0.04 = 1.24$.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: $1.28$ uses $f''(1) = 2$ directly as the coefficient of $(x-1)^2$ without dividing by $2!$, giving $1 + 0.2 + 2(0.04)$.

solution.shortcut: Put $h = x - 1$. Then $x\ln x = (1+h)\left(h - \tfrac{h^2}{2} + \cdots\right) = h + \tfrac{h^2}{2} + \cdots$, and $e^{x\ln x} = 1 + \left(h + \tfrac{h^2}{2}\right) + \tfrac{h^2}{2} + \cdots = 1 + h + h^2 + \cdots$, so the quadratic coefficient is $1$ with no differentiation at all.
solution.commonTrap: Differentiating $x^{x}$ as if it were a power ($x\cdot x^{x-1} = x^{x}$) or dropping the $\tfrac{1}{x}$ that appears when $(\ln x + 1)$ is differentiated. Both give $f''(1) = 1$ and lead to the tempting value $1.22$.

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: MODERATE — one concept (universal quantification in tuple calculus) with four closely related formulas that must be told apart by their quantifier and connective structure; about 2 minutes.
concept: Expressing a division-style ('for every') query in tuple relational calculus with $\forall$ and an implication guard
stem:
A hospital database has the relations $\text{Doctor}(\text{did}, \text{dname})$, $\text{Procedure}(\text{pid}, \text{cat})$ and $\text{Performs}(\text{did}, \text{pid})$. A tuple $(x, y)$ in $\text{Performs}$ records that the doctor with $\text{did} = x$ has performed the procedure with $\text{pid} = y$. Consider the tuple relational calculus query

$$\{\, t \mid \exists d \in \text{Doctor}\,\big(t[\text{dname}] = d[\text{dname}] \wedge \Phi(d)\big) \,\}$$

in which the result tuple $t$ has the single attribute $\text{dname}$ and $\Phi(d)$ is a condition on $d$.

Which one of the following choices of $\Phi(d)$ makes the query return, on **every** database instance, exactly the names of the doctors who have performed every procedure whose category is `'Cardiac'`?

options.label: D
options.text: $\forall p \in \text{Procedure}\,\big(\exists f \in \text{Performs}\,\big(f[\text{did}] = d[\text{did}] \wedge f[\text{pid}] = p[\text{pid}]\big) \Rightarrow p[\text{cat}] = \text{'Cardiac'}\big)$

solution.quick:
'Doctor $d$ performed every Cardiac procedure' means: for all procedures $p$, if $p$ is Cardiac then $d$ performed $p$. That is $\forall p\,(\text{Cardiac}(p) \Rightarrow \text{performed}(d,p))$, which is the first choice.
The $\exists$, $\wedge$ and reversed-implication variants express 'at least one', 'impossible unless every procedure is Cardiac' and 'only Cardiac' respectively.

steps.title: Translate the requirement
steps.body: A doctor $d$ qualifies when, for each procedure $p$ in the database, **if** $p$ has category 'Cardiac' **then** $d$ has performed $p$. Procedures of other categories place no demand on $d$. This is the pattern $\forall p\,(P(p) \Rightarrow Q(d,p))$ with $P(p)$ meaning $p[\text{cat}] = \text{'Cardiac'}$ and $Q$ meaning that a matching tuple exists in $\text{Performs}$.

steps.title: Why the implication is needed
steps.body: $\forall p\,(P \Rightarrow Q)$ is $\forall p\,(\neg P \vee Q)$: a non-Cardiac $p$ makes the bracket true automatically. With $\wedge$ instead, $\forall p\,(P \wedge Q)$ would require **every** procedure to be Cardiac and performed, so a single Neuro procedure in the database makes it false for every doctor.

steps.title: Test all four choices on one instance
steps.body:
Take Doctors Asha, Bilal, Chen, Dev; Procedures 10 (Cardiac), 11 (Cardiac), 12 (Neuro); and Performs: Asha $\to$ 10, 11, 12; Bilal $\to$ 10, 12; Chen $\to$ 10, 11; Dev $\to$ nothing.

| Choice | Meaning | Result on the instance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| first ($\forall$, $\Rightarrow$) | performed every Cardiac procedure | Asha, Chen |
| second ($\exists$, $\wedge$) | performed at least one Cardiac procedure | Asha, Bilal, Chen |
| third ($\forall$, $\wedge$) | every procedure is Cardiac and performed | empty (procedure 12 is Neuro) |
| fourth (reversed $\Rightarrow$) | performed only Cardiac procedures | Chen, Dev (Dev vacuously) |

Only the first choice returns the required set {Asha, Chen}; the others differ already on this instance.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: Correct. $\forall p\,(p[\text{cat}] = \text{'Cardiac'} \Rightarrow \text{doctor } d \text{ performed } p)$ is exactly 'every Cardiac procedure has been performed by $d$'. It is also correctly true for every doctor when there is no Cardiac procedure at all.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: Incorrect. The $\exists$ version only says that $d$ performed **some** Cardiac procedure, so Bilal, who performed only procedure 10 out of the two Cardiac ones, would be returned.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: Incorrect. $\forall p\,(\ldots \wedge \ldots)$ demands that every procedure in the database is Cardiac and performed by $d$; as soon as a non-Cardiac procedure exists the condition fails for every doctor, so the query returns nothing.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: Incorrect. This is the converse implication: every procedure that $d$ performed is Cardiac, i.e. $d$ performs **only** Cardiac procedures. It wrongly accepts a doctor who has performed no procedure at all (Dev) and rejects Asha, who has performed all Cardiac procedures plus a Neuro one.

solution.shortcut: Pattern: 'every $x$ with property $P$ has property $Q$' is always $\forall x\,(P(x) \Rightarrow Q(x))$. A $\wedge$ directly after a $\forall$ is almost always a mistake, and an $\exists$ can only express 'at least one'.
solution.commonTrap: Writing $\wedge$ in place of $\Rightarrow$ under the universal quantifier (a very common slip when translating 'for every Cardiac procedure, the doctor performed it'), or reversing the implication, which turns 'performed all Cardiac procedures' into 'performed only Cardiac procedures'.

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: MODERATE — one concept (single-variable optimisation) in three steps: build the cost function, find the critical point, and notice that it lies outside the permitted interval; about 2.5 minutes.
concept: Minimising a cost function on a closed interval when the unconstrained critical point lies outside it
stem:
A delivery truck must cover a route of $500$ km at a constant speed of $v$ km/h. Running the truck costs $640$ rupees per hour for the driver and overheads, plus a fuel cost of $0.005\,v^{3}$ rupees per hour. Because of a speed restriction on the route, the speed must satisfy $20 \le v \le 32$. Treat $v$ as a continuous variable.

The minimum possible total cost of the trip, in rupees, is ________.

solution.quick:
Total cost $C(v) = \dfrac{500}{v}\,(640 + 0.005v^{3}) = \dfrac{320000}{v} + 2.5v^{2}$. Its only critical point is $v = 40$, which lies outside $[20, 32]$.
Since $C' < 0$ throughout the interval, the minimum is at the right end $v = 32$: $C(32) = 10000 + 2560 = 12560$.

steps.title: Build the cost function
steps.body:
The trip takes $\dfrac{500}{v}$ hours and costs $640 + 0.005v^{3}$ rupees every hour, so

$$C(v) = \frac{500}{v}\,\big(640 + 0.005\,v^{3}\big) = \frac{320000}{v} + 2.5\,v^{2}.$$

steps.title: Find the critical point
steps.body:
$$C'(v) = -\frac{320000}{v^{2}} + 5v = \frac{5v^{3} - 320000}{v^{2}} = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; v^{3} = 64000 \;\Rightarrow\; v = 40.$$

This point lies outside the permitted range $[20, 32]$, so it cannot be used.

steps.title: Locate the minimum on the allowed interval
steps.body: For every $v$ in $[20, 32]$ we have $v^{3} \le 32768 < 64000$, so $5v^{3} - 320000 < 0$ and $C'(v) < 0$. Hence $C$ is strictly decreasing on the whole interval, and its minimum is at the right end point $v = 32$.

solution.commonTrap: Solving $C'(v) = 0$ and stopping at $v = 40$ gives the unconstrained minimum cost $C(40) = 8000 + 4000 = 12000$, which violates the speed limit. On a restricted interval the minimum must be taken over the critical points *inside* the interval and the end points.

v=np.linspace(20,32,120001);i=C(v).argmin()
print(round(v[i],3),round(C(v[i]),2),round(C(40),2))

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: HARD — inclusion–exclusion plus a non-routine insight (relating the pairwise-intersection sum to the 'exactly two' event and removing the triple count), with a likely trap; about 4 minutes.
concept: Inclusion–exclusion for three events and the probability of exactly two occurring

solution.quick:
Inclusion–exclusion gives $0.70 = 3(0.35) - S_2 + 0.05$, so the pairwise sum is $S_2 = \sum_{i<j} P(E_i \cap E_j) = 0.40$.
A unit rejected by exactly two inspections is counted once in $S_2$, but a unit rejected by all three is counted three times. Therefore $P(\text{exactly two}) = S_2 - 3(0.05) = 0.25$.

steps.title: Inclusion–exclusion for the union
steps.body:
$$P(E_1 \cup E_2 \cup E_3) = \sum_i P(E_i) - S_2 + P(E_1 \cap E_2 \cap E_3),\qquad S_2 = \sum_{i<j} P(E_i \cap E_j).$$

Substituting: $0.70 = 3(0.35) - S_2 + 0.05 = 1.10 - S_2$, so $S_2 = 0.40$.

steps.title: Relate $S_2$ to the 'exactly $k$ rejections' events
steps.body:
Let $p_k$ be the probability that exactly $k$ inspections reject. A unit with exactly two rejections lies in exactly one pairwise intersection, while a unit with three rejections lies in all $\binom{3}{2} = 3$ of them. Hence

$$S_2 = p_2 + 3\,p_3.$$

steps.title: Solve for $p_2$
steps.body:
'Exactly three rejections' is the event $E_1 \cap E_2 \cap E_3$, so $p_3 = 0.05$. Then

$$p_2 = S_2 - 3p_3 = 0.40 - 0.15 = 0.25.$$

steps.title: Consistency check
steps.body: $p_0 = 1 - 0.70 = 0.30$ and $p_1 = 0.70 - p_2 - p_3 = 0.40$. The expected number of rejections is $p_1 + 2p_2 + 3p_3 = 0.40 + 0.50 + 0.15 = 1.05 = 3(0.35)$, as it must be, and every $p_k \ge 0$, so the data are consistent and the answer is determined without any assumption about dependence.

solution.shortcut: Let $N$ be the number of rejections, so $E[N] = 3(0.35) = 1.05 = P(N \ge 1) + P(N \ge 2) + P(N \ge 3)$. With $P(N \ge 1) = 0.70$ and $P(N \ge 3) = 0.05$ we get $P(N \ge 2) = 0.30$, and so $P(N = 2) = 0.30 - 0.05 = 0.25$.
solution.commonTrap: Reading $S_2 = \sum_{i<j} P(E_i \cap E_j) = 0.40$ as the probability of 'exactly two'. The sum $S_2$ also counts every unit rejected by all three inspections three times; those $0.05$ must be counted $3 \times 0.05$ and removed.

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: HARD — several iterations of Lloyd's algorithm on eight points, an SSE computation, and the likely trap of assuming that $k$-means reaches the best possible clustering; about 4 minutes.
concept: Sensitivity of $k$-means (Lloyd's algorithm) to the initial centroids: convergence to a local optimum
stem:
The ages (in years) of eight users of a fitness app are

$$20,\quad 22,\quad 29,\quad 30,\quad 38,\quad 39,\quad 41,\quad 42.$$

They are clustered by $k$-means with $k = 2$, using the absolute difference of ages as the distance. The initial centroids are $20$ and $22$. In every iteration each age is assigned to the nearer centroid, and then each centroid is replaced by the mean of the ages assigned to it; the algorithm stops when an assignment step leaves every assignment unchanged. (No age is ever equidistant from the two centroids.) The sum of squared errors (SSE) is the sum, over all eight ages, of the squared difference between the age and the centroid of its cluster.

The SSE of the clustering at which the algorithm stops is (rounded off to two decimal places)

solution.quick:
Starting from $20$ and $22$: iteration 1 gives $\{20\}$ and $\{22,\dots,42\}$ with centroids $20$ and $34.43$; iteration 2 gives $\{20, 22\}$ and $\{29, 30, 38, 39, 41, 42\}$ with centroids $21$ and $36.5$; iteration 3 changes nothing, so the algorithm stops.
SSE $= 2 + 157.5 = 159.5$. This is not the best 2-cluster SSE ($84.75$, for $\{20,22,29,30\}$ and $\{38,39,41,42\}$), because $k$-means only finds a local optimum.

steps.title: Iteration 1
steps.body:
Centroids $20$ and $22$. Ages $20$ goes to the first centroid; every other age ($22, 29, \dots, 42$) is closer to $22$. Clusters: $\{20\}$ and $\{22, 29, 30, 38, 39, 41, 42\}$.

New centroids: $20$ and $\dfrac{22+29+30+38+39+41+42}{7} = \dfrac{241}{7} \approx 34.43$.

steps.title: Iteration 2
steps.body:
The midpoint of the centroids is $\dfrac{20 + 34.43}{2} \approx 27.21$. Ages below it, $20$ and $22$, go to the first cluster; ages above it, $29, 30, 38, 39, 41, 42$, go to the second.

New centroids: $\dfrac{20+22}{2} = 21$ and $\dfrac{29+30+38+39+41+42}{6} = \dfrac{219}{6} = 36.5$.

steps.title: Iteration 3: convergence
steps.body: The midpoint of $21$ and $36.5$ is $28.75$. Age $29$ lies just above it, so it stays in the second cluster, and every other age keeps its cluster. No assignment changes, so the algorithm stops with clusters $\{20, 22\}$ and $\{29, 30, 38, 39, 41, 42\}$ and centroids $21$ and $36.5$.

steps.title: Compare with the best possible clustering
steps.body: The natural split $\{20, 22, 29, 30\}$, $\{38, 39, 41, 42\}$ has centroids $25.25$ and $40$ and SSE $= 74.75 + 10 = 84.75$, which is much smaller. Lloyd's algorithm never moves from the stable clustering it reached, so the bad initial centroids leave it in a local optimum with SSE $159.5$.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: Incorrect. $337.71$ is the SSE of the clusters after only the first assignment step ($\{20\}$ and $\{22, \dots, 42\}$ about $34.43$); the algorithm has not yet converged at that point.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: Correct. The algorithm stops with $\{20, 22\}$ and $\{29, 30, 38, 39, 41, 42\}$, whose SSE is $2 + 157.5 = 159.5$.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: Incorrect. $134.67$ is the SSE of $\{20, 22, 29\}$ and $\{30, 38, 39, 41, 42\}$, which arises only if $29$ is wrongly kept with the first cluster; it is not what the algorithm produces ($29$ is above the midpoint $28.75$).

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: Incorrect. $84.75$ is the global minimum SSE, reached by $\{20,22,29,30\}$ and $\{38,39,41,42\}$. $k$-means does not guarantee it, and the initial centroids $20$ and $22$ lead to a different stable clustering.

solution.commonTrap: Assuming that $k$-means always finds the 'obvious' best split and answering $84.75$. The result depends on the initial centroids; the clustering with centroids $21$ and $36.5$ is stable (no age wants to move), so the algorithm stays there even though a better clustering exists.

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: EASY — one concept (Bayes' theorem with the law of total probability for the denominator) and a single routine computation; about 1.5 minutes.
concept: Posterior probability of plagiarism given a flag, using Bayes' theorem
stem:
A university runs every submitted assignment through a plagiarism checker. Past audits show that $6\%$ of the submissions are plagiarised. The checker flags $90\%$ of the plagiarised submissions, and it also flags $5\%$ of the submissions that are not plagiarised.

A submission is chosen at random and is found to be flagged by the checker. The probability that this submission is actually plagiarised is (rounded off to three decimal places)

solution.quick:
Let $P$ = plagiarised and $F$ = flagged. $P(F) = 0.06(0.90) + 0.94(0.05) = 0.054 + 0.047 = 0.101$.
By Bayes' theorem, $P(P \mid F) = \dfrac{0.054}{0.101} \approx 0.535$.

steps.title: Write down what is given
steps.body: $P(P) = 0.06$, so $P(\bar P) = 0.94$. Also $P(F \mid P) = 0.90$ and $P(F \mid \bar P) = 0.05$. We need $P(P \mid F)$.

steps.title: Apply Bayes' theorem
steps.body:
$$P(P \mid F) = \frac{P(F \mid P)P(P)}{P(F)} = \frac{0.054}{0.101} \approx 0.5347 \approx 0.535.$$

So a little over half of the flagged submissions are genuinely plagiarised, because the small false-flag rate acts on a much larger group of honest submissions.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: Incorrect. $0.900$ is $P(F \mid P)$, the probability that a plagiarised submission is flagged. The question asks for the reverse conditional probability, $P(P \mid F)$.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: Incorrect. $0.054$ is the joint probability $P(P \cap F) = 0.06 \times 0.90$. It has not been divided by $P(F)$, so it is not a conditional probability given the flag.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: Incorrect. $0.947 \approx 0.054 / 0.057$ comes from computing the false-flag part as $0.06 \times 0.05$ instead of $0.94 \times 0.05$, i.e. using $P(P)$ in place of $P(\bar P)$ in the total probability.

solution.shortcut: Think of $1000$ submissions: $60$ are plagiarised, of which $54$ are flagged; $940$ are honest, of which $47$ are flagged. Among the $101$ flagged ones, $54$ are plagiarised, and $54/101 \approx 0.535$.
solution.commonTrap: Answering with the checker's detection rate $0.90$ (confusing $P(F \mid P)$ with $P(P \mid F)$), or forgetting that the false flags come from the $94\%$ honest submissions.

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: HARD — four statements that each need a separate sampling-based computation (prior sampling, rejection sampling, likelihood weighting, Gibbs sampling), with two likely traps; about 5 minutes.
concept: Prior sampling, rejection sampling, likelihood weighting and Gibbs sampling probabilities in a Bayesian network
stem:
A power-distribution monitor is modelled by a Bayesian network over four Boolean variables: $A$ (the grid voltage dips), $B$ (the UPS switches to battery), $C$ (a network switch reboots) and $D$ (the monitoring system raises an outage alert). The edges are $A \to B$, $A \to C$, $B \to D$ and $C \to D$, and the conditional probability tables are:

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| $P(A=1)$ | $0.4$ |
| $P(B=1 \mid A=1)$ | $0.7$ |
| $P(B=1 \mid A=0)$ | $0.2$ |
| $P(C=1 \mid A=1)$ | $0.5$ |
| $P(C=1 \mid A=0)$ | $0.1$ |
| $P(D=1 \mid B=1, C=1)$ | $0.9$ |
| $P(D=1 \mid B=1, C=0)$ | $0.6$ |
| $P(D=1 \mid B=0, C=1)$ | $0.5$ |
| $P(D=1 \mid B=0, C=0)$ | $0.05$ |

(Here $1$ = true and $0$ = false.) The query is $P(A=1 \mid B=1, D=1)$, so the evidence is $B=1$ and $D=1$. In likelihood weighting, the evidence variables are fixed at their observed values and the other variables are sampled in topological order from their tables given their parents. In Gibbs sampling, the evidence variables stay fixed and a non-evidence variable is resampled from its conditional distribution given the current values of **all** the other variables.

Which of the following statements is/are correct?

options.label: A
options.text: In prior (forward) sampling, the probability that one generated sample is exactly $(A, B, C, D) = (1, 1, 0, 1)$ is $0.084$.

options.label: B
options.text: If rejection sampling is run on $N$ prior samples, rejecting every sample that disagrees with the evidence, the expected number of retained samples is $N \cdot P(B=1)\,P(D=1) \approx 0.146\,N$.

options.label: C
options.text: In likelihood weighting, a sample whose sampled values are $A=0$ and $C=1$ receives the weight $P(D=1 \mid B=1, C=1) = 0.9$.

options.label: D
options.text: In Gibbs sampling, when the current state is $(A, B, C, D) = (1, 1, 0, 1)$ and $C$ is resampled, the new value of $C$ is $1$ with probability $0.6$.

solution.quick:
A: the product of the CPT entries is $0.4 \times 0.7 \times 0.5 \times 0.6 = 0.084$, so A is correct. B: $B$ and $D$ are dependent, and the expected retained fraction is $P(B=1, D=1) = 0.2856$, not $0.146$.
C: the weight is $P(B=1 \mid A=0)\,P(D=1 \mid B=1, C=1) = 0.2 \times 0.9 = 0.18$, not $0.9$. D: $P(C=1 \mid A=1, B=1, D=1) \propto 0.5 \times 0.9 : 0.5 \times 0.6$, which gives $0.6$, so D is correct.

steps.title: Statement A: prior sampling
steps.body:
A forward sample draws each variable from its table given its sampled parents, so its probability is the product of the CPT entries:

$$P(A=1)\,P(B=1 \mid A=1)\,P(C=0 \mid A=1)\,P(D=1 \mid B=1, C=0) = 0.4 \times 0.7 \times 0.5 \times 0.6 = 0.084.$$

Statement A is correct.

steps.title: Statement B: rejection sampling
steps.body:
A prior sample is retained exactly when $B=1$ and $D=1$, so the expected retained fraction is $P(B=1, D=1)$, and $B$ and $D$ are dependent because of the edge $B \to D$. Summing over $A$ and $C$:

$$P(B=1, D=1) = \underbrace{0.4(0.7)\big[0.5(0.9) + 0.5(0.6)\big]}_{A=1} + \underbrace{0.6(0.2)\big[0.1(0.9) + 0.9(0.6)\big]}_{A=0} = 0.21 + 0.0756 = 0.2856.$$

Also $P(B=1) = 0.4$ and $P(D=1) = 0.2856 + 0.0786 = 0.3642$, so $P(B=1)P(D=1) \approx 0.146 \ne 0.2856$. Statement B is incorrect.

steps.title: Statement C: likelihood weighting
steps.body:
The weight of a sample is the product, over the evidence variables, of the probability of the observed value given the sampled values of that variable's parents. $B$ has the sampled parent $A$, and $D$ has the parents $B$ (evidence) and $C$ (sampled):

$$w = P(B=1 \mid A=0)\,P(D=1 \mid B=1, C=1) = 0.2 \times 0.9 = 0.18.$$

The factor for $B$ cannot be left out. Statement C, which claims $0.9$, is incorrect.

steps.title: Statement D: Gibbs sampling
steps.body:
The conditional distribution of $C$ given all other variables is proportional to $P(C \mid A)\,P(D \mid B, C)$, the factors that mention $C$ (its own table and its child's table). With $A=1$, $B=1$, $D=1$:

$$C=1:\; 0.5 \times 0.9 = 0.45, \qquad C=0:\; 0.5 \times 0.6 = 0.30.$$

$$P(C=1 \mid A=1, B=1, D=1) = \frac{0.45}{0.45 + 0.30} = 0.6.$$

The current value $C=0$ plays no role. Statement D is correct.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: Statements A and D are correct; B and C are incorrect.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: Correct. The probability of a complete forward sample is the product of the CPT entries along it: $0.4 \times 0.7 \times 0.5 \times 0.6 = 0.084$.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: Incorrect. The retained fraction is $P(B=1, D=1) = 0.2856$. The product $P(B=1)P(D=1) \approx 0.146$ would be valid only if $B$ and $D$ were independent, which they are not (there is an edge $B \to D$).

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: Incorrect. The weight also contains the factor $P(B=1 \mid A=0) = 0.2$ for the evidence variable $B$, whose parent $A$ is sampled; the correct weight is $0.2 \times 0.9 = 0.18$.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: Correct. $P(C=1 \mid A=1, B=1, D=1) \propto P(C=1 \mid A=1)\,P(D=1 \mid B=1, C=1) = 0.45$, against $0.30$ for $C=0$, giving $0.45/0.75 = 0.6$.

solution.commonTrap: In likelihood weighting, multiplying only by the CPT entry of the *last* evidence variable and forgetting that every evidence variable contributes a factor, including one (here $B$) whose parent is a sampled variable. A second trap is multiplying marginals of dependent evidence variables when computing the rejection-sampling acceptance rate.

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: MODERATE — one concept (covariance and variance of linear combinations of uncorrelated variables) with four independent but routine computations; about 3.5 minutes.
concept: Covariance algebra: covariance, correlation and variance of linear combinations of uncorrelated variables
stem:
The noise terms $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ of three sensors are pairwise uncorrelated random variables with $\operatorname{Var}(X) = 4$, $\operatorname{Var}(Y) = 9$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Z) = 1$. Three derived signals are formed:

$$U = X + Y, \qquad V = Y - Z, \qquad T = X - Y.$$

Which of the following statements is/are correct?

options.label: C
options.text: The correlation coefficient $\rho(U, V)$ equals $0.79$, rounded off to two decimal places.

solution.quick:
Because $X, Y, Z$ are pairwise uncorrelated, all cross-covariances vanish: $\operatorname{Var}(U) = 13$, $\operatorname{Var}(V) = 10$, $\operatorname{Cov}(U, V) = \operatorname{Var}(Y) = 9$, so $\rho(U, V) = 9/\sqrt{130} \approx 0.79$.
$\operatorname{Cov}(U, T) = 4 - 9 = -5 \ne 0$, and $2U - 3V = 2X - Y + 3Z$ has variance $16 + 9 + 9 = 34$.

steps.title: Variances and covariance of $U$ and $V$
steps.body:
With zero cross-covariances, $\operatorname{Var}(U) = 4 + 9 = 13$ and $\operatorname{Var}(V) = 9 + 1 = 10$.

$$\operatorname{Cov}(U, V) = \operatorname{Cov}(X + Y,\; Y - Z) = \operatorname{Cov}(X, Y) - \operatorname{Cov}(X, Z) + \operatorname{Var}(Y) - \operatorname{Cov}(Y, Z) = 9.$$

So statement A holds.

steps.title: Correlation of $U$ and $V$
steps.body:
$$\rho(U, V) = \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(U, V)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(U)\operatorname{Var}(V)}} = \frac{9}{\sqrt{13 \times 10}} = \frac{9}{11.40} \approx 0.789 \approx 0.79.$$

So statement C holds.

steps.title: Covariance of $U$ and $T$
steps.body:
$$\operatorname{Cov}(U, T) = \operatorname{Cov}(X + Y,\; X - Y) = \operatorname{Var}(X) - \operatorname{Var}(Y) = 4 - 9 = -5 \ne 0.$$

The sum and the difference of two uncorrelated variables are uncorrelated only when their variances are equal. Here they differ, so statement B is false.

steps.title: Variance of $2U - 3V$
steps.body:
Expand $2U - 3V = 2(X + Y) - 3(Y - Z) = 2X - Y + 3Z$. Since $X, Y, Z$ are pairwise uncorrelated,

$$\operatorname{Var}(2U - 3V) = 2^{2}(4) + (-1)^{2}(9) + 3^{2}(1) = 16 + 9 + 9 = 34.$$

(Check with $4\operatorname{Var}(U) + 9\operatorname{Var}(V) - 12\operatorname{Cov}(U, V) = 52 + 90 - 108 = 34$.) So statement D holds.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: Correct. The only shared term in $U = X + Y$ and $V = Y - Z$ is $Y$, so $\operatorname{Cov}(U, V) = \operatorname{Var}(Y) = 9$.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: Incorrect. $\operatorname{Cov}(U, T) = \operatorname{Var}(X) - \operatorname{Var}(Y) = -5$, so $U$ and $T$ are negatively correlated ($\rho = -5/13 \approx -0.38$).

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: Correct. $\rho(U, V) = 9/\sqrt{13 \times 10} \approx 0.789$, which rounds to $0.79$.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: Correct. $2U - 3V = 2X - Y + 3Z$, whose variance is $16 + 9 + 9 = 34$.

solution.commonTrap: Assuming that $U$ and $T$ (a sum and a difference) are uncorrelated, which is true only when $\operatorname{Var}(X) = \operatorname{Var}(Y)$. A second slip is to compute $\operatorname{Var}(2U - 3V)$ as $4(13) + 9(10) = 142$, forgetting the cross term $-12\operatorname{Cov}(U, V)$ because $U$ and $V$ both contain $Y$.

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: MODERATE — one concept (binary search on a rotated sorted list) traced over four iterations with index arithmetic and a running sum; about 3 minutes.
concept: Binary search for the minimum of a rotated sorted list, traced with a running sum of midpoints
stem:
Consider the following Python function. The list `a` holds distinct integers and is a rotation of a list sorted in increasing order: some number of elements from the front of the sorted list have been moved to the back.

```python
def probe_sum(a):
    lo, hi = 0, len(a) - 1
    acc = 0
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        acc += mid
        if a[mid] > a[hi]:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid
    return acc
```

For `a = [39, 59, 60, 70, 76, 79, 80, 91, 95, 11, 18, 29, 30, 34]`, the value returned by `probe_sum(a)` is ________.

solution.quick:
The loop locates the smallest element (the rotation point), and `acc` adds up the value of `mid` in every iteration.
The four iterations use `mid` = 6, 10, 8, 9 and the loop ends with `lo = hi = 9`, so the function returns $6 + 10 + 8 + 9 = 33$.

steps.title: What the loop does
steps.body: If `a[mid] > a[hi]`, the smallest element must lie to the right of `mid` (the rotation point is in the right half), so `lo = mid + 1`. Otherwise `mid` itself may be the minimum, so `hi = mid`. The loop therefore narrows `[lo, hi]` to the index of the minimum, and `acc` adds up every `mid` that is computed.

steps.title: Result
steps.body: The loop has found the minimum $11$ at index $9$, and the function returns the accumulated sum $6 + 10 + 8 + 9 = 33$. The search needed only $4 = \lceil \log_2 14 \rceil$ iterations, as expected of a binary search.

solution.commonTrap: Returning the number of iterations ($4$) or the final index `lo` ($9$) instead of the sum of the `mid` values, or computing the second `mid` from the stale range (for example using `lo = 6`) because the update `lo = mid + 1` was forgotten. Comparing `a[mid]` with `a[lo]` instead of `a[hi]` also changes the trace.
